newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Hani killer wants to meet victim's wife.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Hani killer wants to meet victim's wife.

text.p: The white rightist jailed for assassinating South African communist leader Chris Hani asked the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission on Friday for permission to meet his victim's family.

Clive Derby-Lewis, 61, a far-right Conservative Party politician who furnished the gun that killed Hani, testified that he had asked to meet his victim's wife Limpho Hani, through his lawyers at the start of his amnesty hearing on Monday.

"I requested permission to meet Mrs Hani in the spirit of reconciliation...I will personally express my sympathy to Mrs Hani and her children," he said as she sat listening in the audience at Pretoria City Hall.
Derby-Lewis and Polish immigrant Janusz Walus, who carried out the killing, were sentenced to death for the 1993 murder and are now, with the death penalty suspended, serving life.

The pair now hope to convince the truth commission, tasked with healing the country's wounds on both sides of the apartheid divide, that they had a political motive for the crime and that they have confessed in full.
But the family of Hani, who was second only to President Nelson Mandela as a popular hero, fiercely opposes freedom for his killers.
Limpho Hani shrugged off Derby-Lewis's comments but did not say she had refused to meet him.
"The statement he made was not for me, it was for the press," she told reporters.
Asked why she had not reacted visibly to his testimony, she said: "What do you expect from someone whose husband was killed in cold blood by the man?"
Derby-Lewis said his detention prior to his trial was his worst experience, describing it as harsher than the military training he had once undergone.
"I have never felt as insecure in my life... I was constantly nervous because I never knew what was coming next," he said.
Derby-Lewis and Walus are seeking to persuade the commission that statements made to police were done so under duress.
The statements, which the Hani family lawyers want to produce at the hearing, apparently contradict the account of the plot he gave in his amnesty application.
Gaye Derby-Lewis, acquitted of complicity in the murder at their trial, has denounced their police interrogators as "professional torturers".

Hani's murder was the most prominent in modern South African history and sent the country to the edge of the abyss, as the plotters had hoped. But Mandela and then president F.W. de Klerk scuppered their hopes by keeping peace talks on track.
Historic elections brought majority rule a year later.
